anchors.fact: Wayne Collins (b. 1970), British bartender from Camden, North London; began pulling pints at a relative's pub in Hoxton in the late 1980s (Proper p. 102; Oxford COLLINS, WAYNE, pdf 557). F1
anchors.meaning: A working bartender behind the bar, not a critic at a desk.

anchors.fact: He "hated the fruit Martini" and wrote an article in *Class* "bashing it" (Proper pp. 101–102). The page gives **no date** for the article; it sits in the chapter's late-1990s London. It doesn't say the article was aimed at LAB or at any one drink. F2
anchors.meaning: A public no to the drink the room loved. The cost on the page is the stand itself. Anything about it costing him warmth is "I like to think".

anchors.fact: *Proper* p. 39: the "red-hot Met Bar" in London "was all about fresh-fruit Martinis"; LAB ("pivotal… in the late 1990s") had its own. p. 98: the Met Bar's fruit "Martinis" "were greeted like a revelation". *Class* was a magazine, published by Simon Difford (p. 39). **Counterweight:** the fruit "Martinis" "made the Martini purists livid, but it kept the cocktail's name alive", and Difford himself argued that the name made it a serious drink (p. 39). F13 (r4, audit R1/R2)
anchors.meaning: The hottest bars poured them, and people loved them. Never "everywhere", and the setting never dates the article. The other side had a case, so nobody is a villain.

anchors.fact: His stated reason: "I didn't like that it was called a Martini" (Proper p. 102, Collins on the record, 2014). F3
anchors.meaning: The objection is to the **name**: a careless thing carrying a name meant to stand for something. Never say he wrote the article for the guests.

anchors.fact: His cocktail schooling came from Lee Chappell (p. 102). In Collins's own quote: "Why would anyone drink gin and vermouth? He'd say, 'You better start liking it. It's not about you, is it? It's about the guests.'" **Speaker:** the outer quote has no tag, but "He'd say" is Chappell, so the voice asking is Collins's, recalling. Tell it as "the way Collins remembers it". "He'd say" is habitual, so no single scene, no date, and no "young" (the page gives no age). F4
anchors.meaning: The standard he later defended wasn't his taste. It was handed to him against his taste, for whoever would drink it, and given with its reason.
anchors.speaksTo: the reason is care, not vanity

anchors.fact: Chappell ran the Long Island Iced Tea Shop in Covent Garden, which served bottled cocktails "at a time when no one else did"; Collins likened him to Bryan Brown's character in *Cocktail* and said he knew five hundred recipes (p. 102). F5
anchors.meaning: The man who taught the gin-and-vermouth rule ran a shop named for a party drink. The standard isn't snobbery. If used, "our reading".

anchors.fact: He kept reading old cocktail books and studied Peter Dorelli (Savoy) and Salvatore Calabrese (Lanesborough) (p. 102); he "grabbed what he could find at book fairs" (p. 60). F6
anchors.meaning: The standard was learned, slowly, out of sight.

anchors.fact: In 2000 chef David Cavalier hired him as bar manager at High Holborn, a forty-seat bar. His menu of classics had "Manhattans, Daisies, and Punches": "I looked for drinks that I found in books that were not on lists around London" (p. 102). F7
anchors.meaning: Say "weren't on other London menus", never "couldn't get anywhere else" (audit R4). Daisies are named as a kind; the whiskey one isn't (R7). The refusal came with a yes: the real one, put in front of people. The position's ground.

anchors.fact: Simonson: "In a time when most London drinkers had never been served a cocktail without ice", Collins was "stirring perfect Sazeracs" in "expensive glassware" (p. 102). The claim is Simonson's, and the glassware is the **Sazeracs'**. F8
anchors.meaning: A Daisy served up in fine glass is **our** choice, said as ours ("the way he served his Sazeracs"), never his Daisy. "Without ice" carries "up"; it doesn't carry "very cold" or "stemmed" (audit R9).

anchors.fact: Of High Holborn: "it influenced a lot of people" (Tony Conigliaro); "An amazing bar to work in" (Sebastian Reaburn, one of his bartenders) (p. 102). The subject is **the bar**, not Collins alone. F9
anchors.meaning: Other people's work got better near it. Robin's rule: say the gift once, plainly.

anchors.fact: Oxford: a key role in the UK bar renaissance of the 1990s, "driving up service standards and improving product knowledge in the industry" with the Mixxit training and education programme he developed (pdf 557). Name Mixxit only as a training programme; the page doesn't date it, so no "went on to" (audit R6). Say "in the trade" or "the industry", not "across the UK". F10
anchors.meaning: The standard became something others were trained to meet.

anchors.fact: Oxford DAISY (pdf 627): "a sour sweetened with a liqueur or flavored syrup, lightened with a splash of sparkling water, and served in a cocktail glass", an American drink of the 1870s, first in print in 1876. In those first printed Daisies the orange cordial is "intended as an accent, not as the main sweetener" (*Imbibe!* pdf 105–106). So by the *Codex*'s structure (p. 106: a small liqueur is seasoning) ours is a **sour, Daiquiri family**. Oxford calls the old Daisy "one of the progenitors of the Sidecar and the Margarita". Daisies were on his High Holborn menu (Proper p. 102). Never the *Codex*'s modern-daisy definition, and never "a Sidecar". Tomás owns the recipe; never "his recipe". F11 (fixed r3, audit H1)
anchors.meaning: Why the drink is an old Daisy: it's the one on his menu that no sibling pours.

anchors.fact: Oxford pdf 627: "Neither version… has been prominent in the twenty-first-century cocktail renaissance" (the book's judgement, 2021). F12
anchors.meaning: Even now it's rarely on a list. Never "nobody makes it".

anchors.fact: Tomás's two teaspoons of vermouth: Chappell's answer to "Why would anyone drink gin and vermouth?" was "You better start liking it" (p. 102). The page never says Collins came to like it, never says *dry*, and the lesson is about gin. The tie is our reading. Taste: Tomás's numbers support "drier" (7.03 → 6.62 g sugar), but not "sharper" (acid 0.828 → 0.793%). (audit T8, R10)
anchors.meaning: The taste he was told to start liking, for someone else.

cocktail.closingLine: Measure the vermouth: it's only two teaspoons. And when you turn something down, add the why.
cocktail.glassware: fine stemmed cocktail glass (about 210 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Chill the glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Put the bourbon, lemon juice, simple syrup, curaçao and dry vermouth in a shaker. Fill it with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds, until the outside of the shaker is almost too cold to hold.
Empty the glass. Strain the drink into it, pouring through a small sieve as well so no chips of ice get in.
Pour the tablespoon of cold soda water on top. No garnish.
cocktail.name: On Their Behalf

recipe.note: any bourbon of 45% (90 proof) or stronger
equal parts sugar and water, stirred until clear
an accent, not the main sweetener, as in the first printed Daisies
a little vermouth, for the gin and vermouth Collins remembers his teacher telling him to start liking: it was for the guests, not for him

cocktail.tagline: You'd rather seem cold than let anyone get the careless version.

reading.epigraph: Two teaspoons of vermouth went in, for a taste one bartender was told to start liking.
whoYouAre: You notice the thing that's slightly off. The line on the page that sits a millimetre low. The dish that should have come out hot. The word on a menu that doesn't mean what it says. Most people let it pass. You can't, and you'd rather seem cold than let it go out like that.

People take it for pride, or for your taste. It isn't, mostly. At the end of every piece of work there's someone who'll never know what you turned down for them, and they're who you're thinking of. You hardly ever mention it, because it sounds like asking to be thanked. So your no arrives alone, without its reason. What you fear is something careless going out under a name that was meant to stand for something. Around you, good becomes normal. People raise their own bar near you, often without noticing they have, and whoever's at the end gets it as it should be.
yours: In 1990s London, the hottest bars were pouring fruit "Martinis". People loved those drinks, and plenty still do. A bartender from Camden called Wayne Collins hated them, and wrote an article against them in a magazine called *Class*. His quarrel was with the name. As he told Robert Simonson in 2014, he didn't like that it was called a Martini.

Here's the part I love. The way Collins remembers it, he'd ask why anyone would drink gin and vermouth, and his teacher, Lee Chappell, would tell him he'd better start liking it, because it was for the guests, not for him. Chappell, by the way, ran a place in Covent Garden called the Long Island Iced Tea Shop. Nobody in this story is a snob.

I can't know what was in Collins's head when he wrote that article, but I like to think it was Chappell's lesson: not his own taste, but a promise made to someone else, about what a name should mean. He didn't stop at no, either. In 2000, as bar manager at High Holborn, he put on a menu of drinks he'd found in old books, ones that weren't on other London menus. That bar, as one London bartender put it, influenced a lot of people, and the training programme he built, Mixxit, is credited with driving up service standards in the trade. That's the shape of what you do: the no comes with a better yes behind it, and people around you start holding the same line.

The cocktail I've made for you is a whiskey Daisy. Daisies were on his High Holborn menu, and I've made this one the old way: whiskey (bourbon, here), fresh lemon, some sugar, just a touch of orange curaçao, then only a splash of soda. It's an old classic you'll still rarely find on a list. I serve it very cold, in a fine stemmed glass. Like his Sazeracs, it comes in good glassware with no ice in it. And I've added two teaspoons of dry vermouth, as a nod to the gin and vermouth Collins was told to start liking, for the guests. You won't taste it as vermouth. You'll taste a drier, rounder drink because of it.

I wouldn't ask you to lower the bar. Please don't, for anyone. But from now on, when you turn something down, add the why, the way Chappell did. A no that comes with its reason stops sounding cold. It sounds like care, because that's what it is. And the reason travels where you can't: people start keeping your standard in rooms you'll never walk into, because at last they understand why.
